title: Inheritance patterns, pedigrees and non-Mendelian traits
objective: Identify autosomal and X-linked inheritance patterns in pedigrees and apply codominance, incomplete dominance and multiple alleles to human traits.
body:
Real families rarely look like a single Punnett square, so health professionals use **pedigrees** and knowledge of inheritance patterns to estimate risk. A pedigree is a family chart in which squares are males, circles are females, shaded shapes are affected people, and half-shaded or dotted shapes often mark **carriers**.

**The four classic single-gene patterns.**
- **Autosomal dominant:** affected people usually have an affected parent; the trait appears in every generation and affects both sexes. An affected heterozygote has a 50% chance of passing it on. Huntington disease and Marfan syndrome follow this pattern.
- **Autosomal recessive:** the trait can skip generations; two unaffected carrier parents can have an affected child. Cystic fibrosis, sickle cell disease and Tay-Sachs disease are examples. **Consanguinity** (parents related by blood) raises the chance of recessive conditions.
- **X-linked recessive:** many more males are affected because males are **hemizygous**, having one X. Affected males inherit the allele from their mother, and fathers cannot pass X-linked traits to sons. Hemophilia A, Duchenne muscular dystrophy and red-green color blindness fit here.
- **X-linked dominant:** affected fathers pass the trait to all daughters and no sons. This pattern is rare.

**Beyond simple dominance.**
- **Incomplete dominance:** the heterozygote shows an intermediate phenotype. Familial hypercholesterolemia is often described this way, because heterozygotes have high cholesterol and homozygotes have far higher levels.
- **Codominance:** both alleles are fully expressed. In the ABO system, I^A and I^B are codominant, giving type AB.
- **Multiple alleles:** a gene has more than two alleles in the population. ABO has three: I^A, I^B and i, with i recessive.
- **Polygenic traits:** many genes add together, often with environment, to produce continuous variation such as height and skin color.

**Mitochondrial inheritance.** Mitochondria carry their own small DNA, inherited almost entirely from the mother. An affected mother can pass a mitochondrial disorder to all her children; an affected father normally passes it to none.

**Reading a pedigree step by step.**
1. Does an affected child have two unaffected parents? If yes, the trait is recessive.
2. Are mostly males affected, with no male-to-male transmission? Consider X-linked recessive.
3. Does it appear in every generation with male-to-male transmission? Think autosomal dominant.

**Most common mistake:** assuming a trait is X-linked just because more males in one small family are affected. Male-to-male transmission rules X-linkage out, so always check whether an affected father has an affected son.
examples: A father with type A blood (I^A i) and a mother with type B blood (I^B i) can have children with type A, B, AB or O blood, each with a 25% chance.
A woman whose father had hemophilia A is an obligate carrier, so each of her sons has a 50% chance of having hemophilia.
In one pedigree, an affected man has an affected son and an affected grandson, which rules out X-linked inheritance and points to an autosomal dominant pattern.

questions.stem: In a pedigree, two unaffected parents have an affected daughter. Which inheritance pattern is most likely?
questions.explanation: Unaffected parents with an affected child means both are carriers of a recessive allele, and an affected daughter with an unaffected father rules out X-linked recessive. Autosomal dominant would require an affected parent.

questions.stem: A man with red-green color blindness and a woman with no affected alleles have a son. What is the son's chance of being color-blind?
questions.explanation: Sons receive their father's Y, not his X, so the son gets an X from his unaffected mother. 50% would apply only if the mother were a carrier.

questions.stem: A person with blood type AB expresses both A and B antigens on red blood cells. This illustrates which concept?
questions.explanation: Both alleles are fully and separately expressed, which is codominance. Incomplete dominance would produce a blended intermediate, not two distinct antigens.

questions.stem: A parent heterozygous for an autosomal dominant condition has a child with an unaffected partner. What is the child's risk of inheriting the condition?
questions.explanation: Aa x aa gives half Aa (affected) and half aa. 25% is the recessive risk for two carriers, not a dominant risk.

questions.stem: A genetic counselor notes that an affected man has an affected son. Which pattern does this rule out?
questions.explanation: Fathers pass their Y, not their X, to sons, so male-to-male transmission excludes X-linked inheritance. Autosomal dominant inheritance routinely shows father-to-son transmission.

questions.stem: A mother has a mitochondrial disorder; the father is unaffected. Which outcome is expected?
choices: All children may inherit the affected mitochondria
questions.explanation: Mitochondria come almost entirely from the egg, so the mother can pass them to all children, regardless of sex. Sex-limited patterns apply to X-linked traits, not mitochondrial ones.

questions.stem: Height varies continuously across a population and is influenced by nutrition. Which term best describes this trait?
questions.explanation: Many genes plus environment produce continuous variation, the hallmark of a polygenic (multifactorial) trait. A single recessive gene would produce distinct categories, not a smooth range.

questions.stem: A woman is a carrier for an X-linked recessive disorder and her partner is unaffected. What fraction of their daughters are expected to be carriers?
questions.explanation: Each daughter gets her father's normal X and a 50% chance of her mother's affected X, so half are carriers. 'All' would be true only if the father were affected.

flashcards.definition: A family chart using standard symbols to track how a trait passes through generations.
An inheritance pattern in which both alleles are fully expressed in the heterozygote, as in type AB blood.
An inheritance pattern in which the heterozygote shows an intermediate phenotype.
Having only one copy of a gene, as males do for most X-linked genes.
A person who has one copy of a recessive disease allele but usually shows no signs of the condition.
